title: Semi-supervised self-training for COVID-19 misinformation detection: analyzing Twitter data and alternative news media on Norwegian Twitter
screen_reason: Although the paper develops a classifier, its substantive contribution is a prevalence estimate over a defined corpus: 5.11% of 426,262 Norwegian-language COVID-19 tweets (21,809 tweets) are classified as misinformation, with a stated denominator. It also reports a hand-labelled prevalence on a stratified random sample (74 of 994 tweets) and an explicit user-level concentration result (25% of the most active users produce about 75% of the misinformation content, Gini 0.61). Detection-method papers are excluded only when the output is model performance; here prevalence, engagement and concentration over a full corpus are the results.

estimates.measure_type: % of Norwegian-language COVID-19 tweets (including retweets) classified as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 426,262 Norwegian-language tweets including retweets (336,553 excluding retweets), collected via the Twitter Academic API with eight COVID-19 keywords plus all tweets sharing those conversation IDs, 1 Jan 2020 - 31 Dec 2022, non-Norwegian tweets and duplicates removed
estimates.definition: A tweet was labelled misinformation (1) or not (0) by a semi-supervised self-training classifier trained on 994 hand-labelled tweets; retweets inherited the label of the original tweet, and the 130,065 tweets the classifier could not predict at the 0.98 confidence threshold were assigned to the non-misinformation class.
estimates.misinfo_def: "In this study, misinformation is defined as any information that is false, inaccurate, or misleading ... defining it as any information that is incorrect, misleading, or false, regardless of the intent of the disseminator."
estimates.source_quote:
This results in a final 
dataset of 426,262 binary classified tweets, with a proportion of 5.11% being classi-
fied as containing misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Section 4.2 (classification results, p. 14) and Section 5.4 (p. 21); also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Semi-supervised self-training with a 0.98 confidence threshold, 19 iterations, seeded with 994 tweets hand-labelled by three annotators (two coded all 994, Cohen's kappa 0.78; a third resolved disagreements; majority voting). Final metrics on the pseudo-labelled sample only: F1 0.9838, precision 0.9987, recall 0.9693. Post-hoc validation: 300 tweets drawn at random from the final dataset and blind-labelled by the author agreed with the classifier at kappa 0.791 (4 mismatches). The author warns that assigning the 130,065 unpredicted tweets to the non-misinformation class 'has the downside of creating a large potential for false negatives'.
estimates.moderator_quote: The final dataset used in this study consists of 426,262 tweets including retweets, and 336,553 excluding retweets.
estimates.notes: Two things an adjudicator should weigh. (1) The denominator INCLUDES retweets, each inheriting the original tweet's label, so the 5.11% is share-weighted rather than a pure count of distinct posts; the corresponding retweet-free denominator (336,553) is reported but no misinformation share is given for it. (2) The estimate is a conservative lower bound by construction: every tweet the classifier could not label at 0.98 confidence (130,065 of them, 31% of the corpus) was assigned to the non-misinformation class, and the author flags the resulting false-negative risk. Year coded 2021 as the midpoint of the three-year window; no annual breakdown is given (Fig. 2 shows monthly distributions only).

estimates.date: January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2022 (25-30 tweets sampled at random per month)
estimates.measure_type: % of hand-labelled Norwegian COVID-19 tweets (retweets excluded) coded as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 74 misinformation and 920 non-misinformation of 994 tweets (7.4%; the percentage itself is not printed, both counts are verbatim)
estimates.denominator: 994 tweets drawn by stratified random sampling (25-30 per month of publication) from the Norwegian COVID-19 corpus after removing retweets
estimates.definition: Each sampled tweet was manually labelled (1) misinformation or (0) not misinformation against the Appendix 1 codebook.
estimates.misinfo_def: "any information that is incorrect, misleading, or false, regardless of the intent of the disseminator"
estimates.source_quote:
After this annotation process, the manually 
labeled sample consisted of 920 tweets classified as not containing any misinforma-
tion, and 74 tweets classified as containing misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three annotators over two rounds: two independently labelled all 994 tweets (Cohen's kappa 0.78, 'substantial'); a third annotator labelled only the disagreements and had the final say; final labels by majority voting.
estimates.moderator_quote: For the manually labeled sample, retweets were removed from the data before a small subset of tweets was extracted using stratified sampling based on the month of publication.
estimates.notes: The HUMAN-coded prevalence on a month-stratified random sample of the same corpus, kept because it is the instrument comparison for the 5.11% classifier row: 7.4% vs 5.11%, consistent with the author's own warning about false negatives. Value is computed as an exact part/whole from two verbatim counts with the same denominator (R8-compliant) but is never printed as a percentage. Retweets are excluded here and included in the classifier row, so the two denominators are not identical. Do not pool both rows: they are the same corpus measured twice.

estimates.measure_type: Share of all COVID-19 misinformation tweets produced by the most active 25% of users
estimates.value_raw: "25% of the most active users contribute to approximately 75% of the misinformation content"; Gini coefficient 0.61
estimates.conc_group_label: Most active 25% of users posting misinformation
estimates.denominator: All 21,809 tweets classified as misinformation, distributed across the users who posted them
estimates.definition: Lorenz curve of misinformation tweets by user; the cumulative share of misinformation tweets attributable to the top quartile of users by misinformation output.
estimates.misinfo_def: "any information that is incorrect, misleading, or false, regardless of the intent of the disseminator"
estimates.source_quote:
centrated among a small proportion of users. As can be seen from Fig.  4, 25% of 
the most active users contribute to approximately 75% of the misinformation con-
tent, providing strong support for the third hypothesis, that the majority of identified

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Concentration computed over the classifier-assigned misinformation labels (same self-training model, F1 0.9838 on the pseudo-labelled sample, validation kappa 0.791).
estimates.moderator_quote: The Gini coefficient for the data is at 0.61.
estimates.notes: R1 satisfied (group size 25% of users AND their 75% share). Note two caveats: the denominator group is users who posted at least one misinformation tweet, not all Twitter users in the corpus, so this is concentration WITHIN misinformation posters; and the 75% figure is read off Figure 4 by the author ('approximately'), not tabulated. The number of users is never stated. Much weaker concentration than the superspreader literature it cites (Grinberg et al.: 0.1% of users, 80% of fake news), partly because the top-25% cut is far broader.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Alternative-news links: 'Out of the 21,809 misinformation tweets in the dataset, 553 (2.5%) contained links to alternative news media sites, while in comparison, of the 404,453 non-misinformation tweets, only 3979 (1%) included such links.' Not extracted as a prevalence row: the numerator is a link to an alternative news outlet, which the paper itself says is not the same as misinformation ('these sites do not always promote misinformation explicitly or even intentionally'); the 2.5% is also a link-type share computed inside the misinformation set. If the review wants a source-level SHARING row for 'share of tweets linking to alternative/low-quality media', the 1% figure for non-misinformation tweets and the 2.5% for misinformation tweets are the verbatim values. 2) Engagement means (misinformation vs non-misinformation: retweets 9.53 vs 4.58, likes 3.60 vs 3.13, replies 0.598 vs 0.531) and the negative-binomial IRRs (0.48 retweets, 0.868 likes, 0.887 replies) are contrasts, not shares of misinformation, so no rows. 3) Classifier performance across the 19 iterations (F1 0.9159 at iteration 4, final 0.9838) is model validation, not prevalence. 4) The monthly temporal peaks (vaccine arrival, Omicron) are shown only as distributions in Figures 2-3 with no dated shares, so the series cannot be collapsed to a dated point beyond the whole-period figure. 5) External statistics cited from other work (Grinberg et al. 0.1% of users / 80% of fake news; the 'Disinformation Dozen' 65%; 21% of Norwegians using social media as a main news source) belong to other studies. 6) Figure 5's top-10 shared domains in misinformation tweets are named (fhi.no, nrk.no) but no domain-level shares are printed.

rob.design: Computational content analysis of a full keyword corpus rather than a sample of people. Frame: Norwegian-language tweets containing any of eight COVID-19 keywords, plus all tweets in the same conversation threads, via the Twitter Academic API, 1 Jan 2020 - 31 Dec 2022; language filtered with cld2, duplicates removed; 426,262 tweets including retweets. Labelling: 994 tweets (25-30 per month, retweets excluded) hand-coded by three annotators against a published codebook, inter-rater kappa 0.78 with a third annotator resolving disagreements; a semi-supervised self-training classifier (0.98 confidence threshold, 19 iterations, fastText embeddings) then labelled the corpus, F1 0.9838 / precision 0.9987 / recall 0.9693 on the pseudo-labelled portion. 130,065 tweets that never met the threshold were assigned to the non-misinformation class, biasing towards false negatives. Blind validation of 300 random classified tweets by the author gave kappa 0.791. Single-platform, single-language, single-country; no human population sampling and no response rate.
rob.item6_quote: In this study, misinformation is defined as any information that is false, inaccurate, or misleading. ... I, therefore, use misinformation as an umbrella term, following Sanaullah et al.
